title: Fed’s Logan favours at least two hikes, says pace could quicken
article:
(Nov 11): Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas president Lorie Logan said she still sees the need for at least two quarter-point rate increases, but that the pace of those hikes may need to be quicker than the Fed is moving this fall.

“It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases,” Logan said on Tuesday in prepared remarks for a conference in Houston, referring to the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on which she votes this year.

While the pace of hikes will depend on economic data and financial conditions, “It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall,” Logan added.

Fed officials left interest rates unchanged at their Oct 27-28 meeting after raising them by a quarter percentage point in September. That was the first rate hike since 2023 as policymakers seek to cool inflation that has been above their 2% target for more than five years.

A majority of officials in September signalled at least one more rate increase would be necessary this year, according to their median projection. While several Fed officials have reinforced this view in recent remarks and said hikes can come at a gradual pace, governor Christopher Waller earlier on Tuesday said the Fed should consider raising rates by a larger, half percentage point at its next meeting in December.

A report released on Tuesday morning showed the consumer price index rose by more than expected in October, with core inflation accelerating at a 0.3% pace from a month earlier. Logan said she’s concerned the Fed’s preferred gauge for inflation, due later this month, could show a similar pickup for October.

See also: US Treasuries drop as hot inflation backs December rate bets

title: IBM to end immigration sponsorship for roles in biggest unit
article:
(Nov 11): International Business Machines Corp (IBM) is ending immigration sponsorship for some roles in its largest division following a crackdown by the Trump administration on a visa programme that’s been a talent pipeline for the tech industry.

“We have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting,” an IBM spokesperson said.

Impacted workers can continue working with IBM outside the US, or leave the company at the end of the year, according to a document shared with managers this week in that division seen by Bloomberg. Consulting is by far IBM’s largest division, with over 150,000 workers, according to its website.

The technology industry’s reliance on foreign workers has long been a flashpoint in the debate over immigration. Since President Donald Trump’s return to office last year, the administration has seized on those concerns and pressed tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers.

As part of that effort, Trump has moved to make it harder for companies to use H-1B visas to attract foreign talent. The changes have included proposals for US$100,000 filing fees for most candidates and tightening the rules of how the H-1B visas are awarded in an annual lottery, giving priority to companies offering the highest salaries.

See also: US stocks slide after hot inflation boosts December rate hike bets

Last month the administration accused Microsoft Corp, Adobe Inc and a half-dozen other companies of abusing a US worker visa programme and suspended them indefinitely from using it.

The affected IBM division participated “US high-skilled visa programmes” to address skill shortages, the spokesperson said. But participation has been declining for a number of years and skill availability and client need have evolved, the spokesperson said.

Big Blue has refashioned itself as a high-growth software company through major acquisitions of Red Hat, HashiCorp and Confluent. At the same time, its consulting business has lagged — the division’s growth has been largely flat since 2024.
